opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it shaped expectations enormously, and mostly in a misleading direction. There's this famous story from the early days of AI. In the 1960s, Marvin Minsky at MIT supposedly assigned an undergraduate a summer project to connect a camera to a computer and get it to describe what it saw. The assumption was that vision was the easy part. The hard parts, the things that signaled real intelligence, were supposed to be chess, theorem proving, and solving calculus problems. Those were the things that took smart people years to master.

It turned out to be almost exactly backwards. This is what people call Moravec's paradox: the things we find hard, like playing grandmaster-level chess, turned out to be relatively easy for computers, and the things a two-year-old does effortlessly, like recognizing a face, picking up a cup, or understanding that an object behind a couch hasn't stopped existing, turned out to be enormously difficult.

I think the reason is that perception feels effortless to us precisely because it's not available to introspection. We have no conscious access to the massive amount of processing our brains are doing. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years refining those systems, and they run below the level of awareness. So when you look at a scene and just *see* a dog on a sofa, it seems like there's nothing to explain. And if there's nothing to explain, it seems like there should be nothing hard to build.

That illusion persists even now. When deep learning systems started doing well on benchmarks like ImageNet, a lot of people declared that object recognition was essentially solved. But when you probe these systems, you find they're often relying on shortcuts, like texture rather than shape, or background cues, or statistical correlations in the dataset, and they can be fooled by small perturbations no human would notice. Human perception is deeply entangled with everything else we know: our understanding of physics, of intentions, of what objects are for, of how scenes are typically organized. Seeing is really a form of understanding, and I think we're still underestimating how much of our general cognition is involved in what feels like simply opening our eyes.

So the lesson I take from that history is a kind of humility: when something seems easy to us, that's often a sign that we don't understand how we do it, not that it's simple.

r001.rationale: The response says early AI researchers assumed vision was the easy part, and explains that because perception feels effortless and its processing is hidden from introspection, it seemed easy to build in machines.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it shaped them enormously, and mostly in the direction of overconfidence. There's this famous story from 1966 where Marvin Minsky assigned computer vision to an undergraduate as a summer project. The thinking was, essentially, that vision is something we do effortlessly, without any conscious thought, so how hard could it be? Compare that to chess or theorem proving, which felt like the pinnacle of human intellect. The early pioneers assumed the hard problems for AI would be the ones that are hard for people, and the easy ones would be the ones that are easy for people.

And of course it turned out to be almost exactly backwards. This is what Hans Moravec later called Moravec's paradox: the things that took evolution hundreds of millions of years to get right, like perceiving a scene, recognizing an object from a new angle, picking up a cup, are enormously hard to engineer, while the things humans find difficult, like playing chess, turned out to be comparatively tractable. The reason perception feels easy is precisely because so much of the machinery is hidden from us. We have no introspective access to how we recognize a face or segment a scene into objects. So the apparent ease was really an illusion created by our own lack of insight into what our brains are doing.

I'd add that this pattern keeps recurring. Every generation of AI seems to rediscover it. Deep learning got us huge gains on benchmarks like ImageNet, and there was a lot of talk about vision being "solved." But then you look at adversarial examples, or at how these systems fail when you change the context slightly, or ask them to understand what's actually happening in a scene rather than just labeling objects, and you realize the gap between labeling and genuine understanding is still very wide. Perception for us is deeply tied to concepts, to our bodies, to our expectations about how the world works. We don't just detect patterns; we make sense of things. And I think the original mistake, assuming that something effortless must be simple, is one we're still a bit prone to.

r001.rationale: The response says early AI pioneers treated vision as easy to reproduce because people perform it effortlessly, asking “how hard could it be?” and assuming tasks easy for people would also be easy for AI.

astra-6.text:
I think it led us to underestimate the problem enormously. When you look at a scene, you immediately recognize the objects, you have some sense of what’s happening, and you don’t experience all the processing that makes that possible. So it’s very natural to think, well, how hard could that be to program?

Whereas something like playing chess or proving a theorem feels difficult. It takes conscious effort, and we associate it with intelligence. So the early expectation was that those would be the hard problems, and seeing and recognizing things would be relatively straightforward. In many ways, it turned out to be the reverse.

The lesson is that what feels effortless to us isn’t necessarily computationally simple. Perception draws on a tremendous amount of knowledge and experience, much of which we can’t articulate. And that makes it very hard to capture by simply writing down rules.

r001.rationale: The response says perception feels immediate and effortless, leading early researchers to think seeing and recognition would be relatively straightforward to program.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it led us to underestimate the problem enormously. When you look at a scene, you immediately recognize the objects, what people are doing, and perhaps what’s likely to happen next. It feels effortless, so it’s natural to think that it must be relatively easy to program. But we don’t have conscious access to all the processing that makes that possible.

Early AI researchers tended to focus on things we consider intellectually difficult, like playing chess or proving theorems. And those turned out to be much more tractable than many things a young child can do. Everyday perception draws on a tremendous amount of knowledge about the world. So I think the apparent ease of perception hid precisely the complexity that AI needed to explain.

r001.rationale: The response says perception feels effortless, making it natural to think it would be relatively easy to program, and explains that this apparent ease hid its complexity from early AI.
